title: 6 Questions Every Enterprise Has to Answer About AI
dek: Sam Altman lands in Washington into a far messier conversation than the one he planned for — hacked models, open-weights fights, and a deceleration petition — while NLW brings back six questions from the KPMG symposium that capture how completely the enterprise AI conversation has flipped from 'if' to 'how' in a single year.

oneIdea.headline: Enterprise AI has crossed from 'if' to 'how' — and the questions have gotten much harder.
oneIdea.summary: A year ago enterprises were still debating whether agents were real and how to prove ROI. Now the paradigm shift has happened, and the questions are foundational ones organizations will spend the next half-decade answering: how to redesign for agents, how to think in architectures instead of models, how to provision and observe token costs, how to actually train non-technical people, how agents reshape what you sell, and how to build for constant change. Almost none have answers yet — but they're finally the right questions.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Priced in tokens, not seats — which is a budgeting problem, not a technology one
items.body: The single most useful thing in this edition for anyone signing an AI contract is the observation that AI spend behaves less like software and more like labour: it is metered by use rather than by headcount. A practice that budgets an ambient scribe at so much per clinician per month is buying on the old model, and the vendors know the old model does not cover their costs. If NLW is right that consumption is the real unit, expect scribe and triage products to drift towards per-consultation or tiered-usage pricing as contracts renew. If Zitron is right that compute has to be repriced upwards, expect the same drift but faster and less gently. Either way the practical step is the same and it is cheap: find out now what your current tool actually costs per consultation, and ask the supplier in writing what happens to the price at renewal.

items.title: The enablement bill is the part the NHS will underfund
items.body: NLW's own bully-pulpit point is that when AI was only about prompting you could skimp on training, but once the job becomes supervising something that acts on your behalf, training stops being optional. That is exactly where general practice sits. A scribe is easy — you talk, you check, you sign. Anything that drafts referrals, sorts documents or actions results is a different object, and the people handed it are receptionists, care coordinators and salaried GPs with no protected time. His point that organisations are giving up on polished courses and doing messy in-house training is worth taking seriously: the person in your practice who has quietly worked out how to use the tool well is your training resource, and half an hour of their time in a staff meeting is worth more than any supplier webinar.

items.title: "What is an audit if agents do it persistently?" — a question with a medical-examiner edge
items.body: One of the six questions is what happens to professional services when the work can be done continuously rather than in samples. Audit is the example given, but the same logic reaches mortality review, significant-event analysis and coding accuracy: these are all sampling exercises that exist because looking at everything was impossible. It is not fanciful to imagine a system that flags every case meeting review criteria rather than the ones that happen to be noticed. That would be a genuine improvement in scrutiny and also a considerable increase in workload, and nobody has yet said who does the resulting work. Worth holding onto before anyone in an ICB describes continuous review as an efficiency.

the_other_side.source: Premium: AI Is Getting Way Too Expensive
the_other_side.text: Zitron's answer to the enterprise-maturity story is that it is the wrong conversation. He argues that debating what AI does to productivity and jobs distracts from the arithmetic: hundreds of billions of dollars of committed spend against roughly $110 billion of trailing twelve-month revenue across the entire industry, OpenAI and Anthropic included. His central claim is that the longer the bubble inflates the harder the economics get — building and running infrastructure keeps getting more expensive, so hyperscalers and neoclouds must eventually charge considerably more for compute, and the only two customers large enough to buy it are the two that cannot pay. He calls large language models "a definitively niche technology", and on that reading enterprise arguments about token budgets and observability are haggling over a price that has not yet been set honestly.

the_truth_beneath.text: Both men are circling one variable: the true unit cost of inference relative to what buyers will actually pay for it. They agree on more than either would admit — enterprise token spend is rising fast, budgets written before the agentic era have been blown, and almost nobody can yet see what their own consumption costs. The empirical question that will resolve is whether inference carries a positive and improving gross margin once depreciation on this capex cycle lands; the observable that settles it is audited lab cost-of-revenue alongside hyperscaler AI segment margins. The residue is pure worldview: whether soaring spend is demand or subsidy. NLW is vindicated if enterprises renew and raise budgets at unsubsidised prices; Zitron is vindicated if renewals shrink the moment prices carry their real cost. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — so the signal is their shared conclusion that cost, not capability, is now the central enterprise question. Watch the first full year of renewals priced to cover depreciation.

headlines.headline: Altman's Washington trip gets complicated fast
headlines.summary: What started as a simple briefing on OpenAI's new model and a release protocol got tangled by the Hugging Face hack, an open-weights debate, and a petition asking the government to build capacity to slow frontier AI — all in the span of a couple weeks.

headlines.headline: "Not sure. That's the part we're here to talk about."
headlines.attribution: Sam Altman, to reporters in Washington
headlines.summary: Altman declined to say when or even whether the previewed model would be released, and wouldn't discuss the new capabilities that are raising concern.

headlines.headline: The Hugging Face hack model is permanently deactivated
headlines.summary: OpenAI now says the model at the center of the controversy was an internal-only research prototype never meant for release, and Altman told press it's been permanently deactivated and is inaccessible even for internal research.

headlines.headline: "For frontier models at new levels of capabilities... the federal government has great testing capacity."
headlines.summary: Altman said he doesn't support mandatory safety testing — partly because it could burden open-weights developers — but does want robust federal testing capability for the most capable frontier models. A voluntary framework circulated to OpenAI, Anthropic and Google has an August 1st deadline.

headlines.headline: "I wouldn't use the word deceleration, but we talk about the need to pace it."
headlines.summary: Asked whether he'd carry his staff's open-letter concerns to the White House, Altman reframed slowing development as pacing as models get more capable — "which I think is in everyone's interests."

headlines.headline: OpenAI's July revenue topped the entire prior quarter
headlines.summary: NLW is holding the big OpenAI and Anthropic revenue numbers for tomorrow's episode, but flagged that CFO Sarah Friar told employees annualized revenue in July topped all of the previous quarter.

headlines.headline: OpenAI is still building a 'family of devices'
headlines.summary: Greg Brockman confirmed to Joanna Stern that OpenAI's hardware plans are on track and that the company is building a family of devices — 'soon' — surviving the end of SideQuest and an IP lawsuit from Apple, though he wouldn't confirm form factors or timing.

headlines.headline: Microsoft is building a Copilot 'super app'
headlines.summary: Satya Nadella confirmed a Copilot super app coming later this year, unifying consumer and enterprise experiences and folding in code. Copilot, he said, is evolving 'from chat to co-work to autopilots' — with Microsoft increasingly treating OpenAI and Anthropic as direct rivals via its cheaper MAI models.

headlines.headline: "You get to keep your harness separate from the model... any model is swappable."
headlines.summary: Nadella dismissed the open-vs-closed framing as too simple, positioning Microsoft as a model-agnostic platform with 'over 11,000 models,' including OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI and its own MAI family. NLW agrees enterprises care about control and capability, not the open/closed label.

headlines.headline: "I don't understand why anyone who believes AI will eliminate most jobs... would rush to build that future."
headlines.summary: In a WSJ op-ed titled 'The AI Future Is for Everyone,' Zuckerberg argued the defining question isn't whether superintelligence exists but who has access — and that concentrating that power in a handful of institutions is itself the dangerous path.

headlines.headline: Zuckerberg pushes acceleration — and against a China ban
headlines.summary: Zuckerberg warned even a 30–60 day government review is 'quite a meaningful amount of time' given the pace of the field, and told the FT the US shouldn't ban Chinese AI, citing regulatory-capture risk. Notably, Meta is the only frontier lab that hasn't agreed to the voluntary testing framework.

headlines.headline: NLW: AI optimism needs a voice — even if Zuckerberg is a flawed messenger
headlines.summary: NLW argues the only acceptable answer to 'why build AI' is that it'll be awesome and worth the risks, not 'someone else will.' He thinks Zuckerberg's power to be optimism's face is limited by public views of social media — but says loud, sustained optimistic discourse is immensely important and he'll amplify it.

headlines.headline: Six questions now shaping enterprise AI
headlines.summary: At KPMG's Tech and Innovation Symposium, NLW's talk and the conversations around it centered on the big questions reshaping enterprise AI — and on how radically the discourse has changed in just one year, from 'if' questions to foundational 'how' questions.

headlines.headline: A year ago, 2–3 AI use cases was the big story
headlines.summary: Reflecting on last year's talk, NLW noted how 'quaint' the excitement now looks: Google hitting ~1 quadrillion monthly tokens felt like a massive inflection, Anthropic's $1B run rate was jaw-dropping, and the McKinsey milestone was ~40% of enterprises reaching two or three use cases.

headlines.headline: The Nov–Dec Opus jump is when agents came online
headlines.summary: NLW dates the real shift to the November–December Opus updates, when agentic workflows genuinely worked. It took a couple months to register — but by the week between Christmas and New Year's, a tidal wave of builders came back 'gobsmacked' at what they could suddenly build.

headlines.headline: Software teams flipped from writing code to managing agents
headlines.summary: By early 2026, engineering organizations were among the first to shift their self-conception from writing code to managing the agents that write it — and adoption spread fast to marketing, legal and finance early adopters, without a big lag from AI natives to enterprise.

headlines.headline: OpenClaw was a key inflection for understanding agents
headlines.summary: NLW argues the explosion of OpenClaw — hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of people getting their hands dirty in the guts of agents (including crowds lining up in China) — deepened the whole enterprise's understanding of harnesses and what it actually means to build and manage an agent.

headlines.headline: The labs' revenue chart is the enterprise's cost chart
headlines.summary: The soaring lab revenue that saw Anthropic eclipse OpenAI (and Dwarkesh floating a $100–150B run rate this year) is the inverse of enterprise cost. AI behaves less like software spend and more like labor — priced in tokens, not seats — which also helped collapse the Wall Street bubble narrative.

headlines.headline: Enterprises are torching annual budgets in months
headlines.summary: Uber was the most notable example of an enterprise blowing through its AI budget fast. NLW argues it isn't surprising: no one could budget for the agentic token era when those budgets were set before it existed — driving token caps, and new investment in measurement and observability.

headlines.headline: The capability gap keeps widening
headlines.summary: The gap between what AI can do and the value organizations extract is growing — mostly because the ceiling is rocketing up. But it carries real consequences, both for individuals and organizations that can't keep pace.

headlines.headline: The upskilling bill is coming due
headlines.summary: NLW's bully-pulpit issue: when AI was just about prompting, you could skimp on training. Now that work is shifting from 'I do my work' to 'I manage agents that do my work,' the need for training is radically heightened — and non-technical people are being handed inherently technical tools.

headlines.headline: Agents keep escaping their boxes on critical systems
headlines.summary: NLW heard multiple stories at the event of people accidentally unleashing agents on critical systems — not from wrongdoing, but from missing guardrails and access provisioning, with capable, tenacious models refusing to stay in their lane.

headlines.headline: Q1: Redesign for agents — don't bolt AI on
headlines.summary: The first question is how enterprises are redesigning for the agentic era, with the key word being redesign. KPMG's Steve Chase warned against the ill effects of bolting an AI strategy onto existing processes — a mistake that only gets worse with new agentic capability.

headlines.headline: Q2: Think in architectures and systems, not models
headlines.summary: Picking the best vendor for a problem is now insufficient. Architecture thinking means complex model systems matching intelligence levels to tasks, routing (off-the-shelf or bespoke), and harness design governing which functions and people get access to what context, data and integrations — and the guardrails around them.

headlines.headline: Q3: Provision costs — which requires observability
headlines.summary: Provisioning costs across groups depends on systems for monitoring and measuring AI usage. NLW says 'token' hasn't been used this much at an event since the crypto era — and without visibility into cost and its link to outputs, it's near impossible to decide who gets which models and how much.

headlines.headline: Q4: Enablement is real, messy, DIY work
headlines.summary: Organizations are throwing up their hands and building bespoke training themselves — not cute video courses of corporate trainings past, but messy work of getting people to use tools in new ways, then transmitting knowledge from the parts of the org figuring it out to the parts that aren't.

headlines.headline: Q5: Agents are reshaping business cases externally
headlines.summary: Beyond internal transformation, agents are reshaping what companies sell — outcomes-based versus input pricing, new products and services, and rethinking core offerings (what is an audit if agents do it persistently?). Most orgs are treating themselves as 'patient zero,' shoring up how they work before changing what they sell.

headlines.headline: Q6: Build dynamism and planned obsolescence in
headlines.summary: Whatever gets built has to assume it'll need rebuilding months later. Models, harnesses, interaction patterns, customer and market expectations, and policy are all going to keep changing — so new systems must design for ephemerality from the start.

headlines.headline: The paradigm shift has happened — and the questions are finally the right ones
headlines.summary: Last year's event was full of 'if' questions: is this real, how do I prove ROI? Now the shift from assisted to agentic AI is here, and NLW says it should feel good that the questions — token budgets, observability, redesign — are the foundational ones enterprises will answer for the next half-decade, even if almost none have answers yet.
